title: Australia experiencing rampant tooth decay as millions delay dentistry

TOK PISIN

By Peter Lusted

Topic:Dental Care

Student Emily Novo ended up in a hospital emergency department after a bacterial infection in her mouth. (ABC News: Warwick Ford)

Dentists say one-third of adults are experiencing tooth decay, with many patients also citing an inability to afford dentistry.

Dozens of dentists are at Parliament House in Canberra to warn politicians that delayed dental issues become worse and more expensive to treat.

The federal government has not yet finalised its National Oral Health Plan 2025 to 2034, despite dentists consulting on it in 2024.

Emily Novo was brushing her teeth before bed when she felt a slight pain above one of her wisdom teeth.

She woke up the next day and could not open her mouth.

"I couldn't even open it enough to brush my teeth, let alone eat a piece of toast," the Sydney student said.

She went to her general practitioner who could not get access to her mouth and sent her to a hospital emergency department.

Student Emily Novo says she did not prioritise going to the dentist after moving out of home, due to the cost. (ABC News: Warwick Ford)

Ms Novo was stressed about the health implications, and as a student she feared what it might cost.

"From a cost point of view, it was really, really daunting," she said.

"Because of my age ... they decided to go against any X-rays or putting me under any sort of radiation, and they felt comfortable enough to send me home with some hardcore antibiotics."

Young Australians are living with untreated dental issues as they’re also bombarded with dubious social media advice.

Fortunately for Ms Novo, the antibiotics eventually worked. But she was unable to open her mouth properly for a week.

"I was just eating soup all week, I couldn't eat properly, I couldn't talk properly," she said.

Ms Novo said she generally had good oral health, but the issue came from bacteria getting into the cavity between her wisdom tooth and gum.

She said she had put off going to the dentist because of the cost, but the incident had been a wake-up call.

"So in hindsight, I really should have prioritised my … dental hygiene," she said.

Dr Angie Nilsson says she fears young people are undergoing risky, quick fixes to their dental issues. (ABC News: Luke Stephenson)

According to an Australian Dental Association (ADA) survey, more than 2 million Australians have skipped dental care due to unaffordability.

ADA vice president Angie Nilsson said that had resulted in widespread tooth decay.

"The issue that we've got is if people aren't going to a dentist early, it ends up becoming more expensive, more painful, they have to take more time off work," she said.

Dentists meet at Parliament House in Canberra to lobby politicians for progress on a national plan. (Supplied: Australian Dental Association)

More than 40 dentists from around the country have gathered in Canberra this week to alert politicians to the nation's dental problems.

Dr Nilsson said other issues included a lack of access to dentistry in regional areas, and young people following bad dental advice.

"60 per cent of 18 to 25-year-olds are making decisions based on social media, and that can lead to use of bleaching that can be unhealthy for them, can damage their teeth," she said.

Dentists said the solution was to implement a national plan.

Consultations took place with dentists in 2024 for the National Oral Health Plan 2025 to 2034, which was due to be put to a health ministers' meeting that year.

However, the ADA said the federal government had since delayed the plan's release.

"The National Oral Health Plan is giving us that framework to be able to say, 'Okay, well here is the problem, we know what the problem is, we need to be able to co-design these solutions so that we can improve the oral health of all Australians,'" Dr Nilsson said.

Dr Chris Sanzaro says dental care should not be seen as a "luxury". (ABC News: Luke Stephenson)

ADA president Chris Sanzaro said oral health could no longer be separate to mainstream health policy.

"A National Oral Health Plan is not a luxury; it is essential to giving Australians the access to care they deserve."
